group.title: Cities and housing
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A tall, narrow house joined to similar houses in a row.
examples: They live in a three-story {townhouse} near the park.
wrong: Our townhouse stands alone in a field with no other houses nearby.

words.meaning: To rent out a home you are renting yourself to another person.
examples: She {sublet} her apartment while she worked abroad.
wrong: He sublet his apartment by living in it alone all year.

words.meaning: A person who owns the house or apartment they live in.
examples: Every {homeowner} on the street pays the local tax.
wrong: As a homeowner, she pays rent to a landlord every month.

words.meaning: A short street that is closed at one end.
examples: The kids play safely in the quiet {cul-de-sac}.
wrong: A cul-de-sac is a busy highway that goes on for miles.

words.meaning: A person who travels regularly, often a long way, between home and work.
examples: The early train is full of {commuters}.
wrong: A commuter is someone who never leaves the house.

words.meaning: Too much traffic or too many people in one place.
examples: {Congestion} in the city center is worst at 8 a.m.
wrong: There was no congestion, and the roads were jammed with cars.

words.meaning: Rules that control what can be built in each part of a town.
examples: {Zoning} laws keep factories away from homes.
wrong: Zoning means anyone can build anything anywhere.

words.meaning: A very tall building in a city.
examples: From the top of the {skyscraper}, you can see the whole bay.
wrong: The skyscraper was a tiny one-story hut.

words.meaning: Very tall, with many floors.
examples: They live on the 30th floor of a {high-rise} apartment building.
wrong: The high-rise building has only one floor.

words.meaning: Of a house: standing alone, not joined to another house.
examples: They bought a {detached} house with a big yard.
wrong: Our detached house shares walls with the houses on both sides.

words.meaning: To repair and improve an old building so it is in good condition.
examples: They {renovated} the old farmhouse.
wrong: They renovated the house by letting it fall apart.

words.meaning: The work of keeping a building or machine in good condition.
examples: The rent includes building {maintenance}.
wrong: Regular maintenance is what makes a building fall apart.

words.meaning: Services such as electricity, gas and water supplied to a home.
examples: The rent is $900 a month, plus {utilities}.
wrong: Utilities are the paintings you hang on the walls.

words.meaning: Of a home: rented with furniture already in it.
examples: We rented a {furnished} apartment, so we didn’t need to buy a bed.
wrong: The furnished apartment was completely empty, with no furniture.

words.meaning: Too small for the people or things inside.
examples: Six of us shared a {cramped} two-room apartment.
wrong: The cramped room had plenty of space for everyone.

words.meaning: Having a lot of room inside.
examples: The new office is bright and {spacious}.
wrong: The spacious kitchen was so small two people couldn’t fit.

words.meaning: Having too many people in a place.
examples: The trains are {overcrowded} at rush hour.
wrong: The overcrowded bus had only two passengers.

words.meaning: Connected with towns and cities.
examples: {Urban} areas often have better public transportation.
wrong: Urban life means living on a remote farm far from any town.

words.meaning: Connected with the countryside, not towns.
examples: She grew up in a {rural} village with one shop.
wrong: The rural area was full of skyscrapers and subway stations.

words.meaning: The spread of a city into the countryside around it, often without a plan.
examples: {Urban sprawl} has swallowed up the farmland near the city.
wrong: Urban sprawl means the city is getting smaller and more compact.

words.meaning: Useful places and services in an area, such as shops, parks and pools.
examples: The apartment is close to all local {amenities}.
wrong: The area has great amenities: no shops, no parks and no buses.

words.meaning: The change in a poor area as richer people move in and prices rise.
examples: {Gentrification} has pushed many longtime residents out of the area.
wrong: Gentrification made the neighborhood cheaper and poorer.

words.meaning: To legally force someone to leave the home they rent.
examples: The family was {evicted} for not paying rent.
wrong: The landlord evicted them by inviting them to stay longer.

words.meaning: To move to a new place to live or work.
examples: The company {relocated} us to another city.
wrong: They relocated, so they stayed exactly where they were.

words.meaning: Money you pay a landlord before moving in, returned if you cause no damage.
examples: We got our {security deposit} back when we moved out.
wrong: The security deposit is the monthly payment for electricity.

words.meaning: Land and buildings that people buy and sell.
examples: She works in {real estate}, selling houses.
wrong: Real estate means cars and boats that you can drive.

words.meaning: The older central parts of a big city, often poor and crowded.
examples: The charity runs youth clubs in the {inner city}.
wrong: The inner city is a quiet village far out in the countryside.

words.meaning: Connected with a large city and the areas around it.
examples: The {metropolitan} area has over five million people.
wrong: The metropolitan region is a tiny village with fifty people.

words.meaning: Run by or belonging to a town or city government.
examples: The {municipal} pool is free for residents.
wrong: The municipal library is owned by one family and run for profit.

words.meaning: A person who shares a room or apartment with you.
examples: My {roommate} and I split the rent.
wrong: My roommate lives alone in another city, and we have never shared a home.

words.meaning: Looking for a home to buy or rent.
examples: We spent the weekend {house-hunting} in the suburbs.
wrong: They went house-hunting to look for a new car.

words.meaning: In bad condition because nobody has looked after it.
examples: They bought a {run-down} cottage and fixed it up.
wrong: The run-down hotel was brand new and spotless.

words.meaning: Looked after carefully and in good condition.
examples: The street is lined with {well-kept} gardens.
wrong: The well-kept house had broken windows and weeds everywhere.

words.meaning: Having few inside walls, so rooms flow into one large space.
examples: The apartment has an {open-plan} kitchen and living room.
wrong: The open-plan office is divided into dozens of small closed rooms.

words.meaning: A person who lives in a particular place.
examples: The town has about 20,000 {inhabitants}.
wrong: The inhabitants of the island have never been there.

words.meaning: An old house in poor condition, sold cheaply to someone who will repair it.
examples: They bought a {fixer-upper} and spent a year repairing it.
wrong: The fixer-upper was in perfect condition and needed no work at all.

words.meaning: To move to a smaller home, often after children have left.
examples: After the kids left, they {downsized} to an apartment.
wrong: They downsized from a studio to a ten-bedroom mansion.

words.meaning: To start to feel comfortable in a new home or place.
examples: It took the kids a few weeks to {settle in}.
wrong: She settled in quickly, so she felt lost and uneasy for months.

words.meaning: The idea of buying a cheap home first, then more expensive ones later.
examples: Young people struggle to get on the {property ladder}.
wrong: The property ladder is the ladder you use to paint the ceiling.

words.meaning: A very poor, crowded area of a city with bad housing.
examples: The project replaced the {slum} with safe new homes.
wrong: The slum was the richest, most luxurious part of town.
